summary:
Tanzania criminalises same-sex sexual conduct. The Penal Code as revised by the Sexual Offences (Special Provisions) Act 1998 provides a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for same-sex acts between men; section 138A treats "gross indecency" as an offence carrying one to five years' imprisonment or a fine of TSh 100,000 to 300,000. Heterosexual oral and anal sex are also offences under the same framework.

The semi-autonomous jurisdiction of Zanzibar, governed by its own House of Representatives, runs a separate criminal statute. The Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 defines "gross indecency" broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute below 12, with under-18 and marriage distinctions) and provides penalties including three years' imprisonment. Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934, as amended in 2004, outlaws sex between women with up to five years' imprisonment or a TSh 500,000 fine.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition anywhere in Tanzania, so no partner can be sponsored, inherited from, or recognised as next of kin through relationship status. Adoption requires a married couple, so a same-sex couple cannot adopt jointly.

Documented violence against LGBT people includes a June 2024 attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo, abducted by 12 men and found beaten in a forest with her ears cut; the UN Human Rights Office condemned the attack as "horrendous" and flagged possible violations of ICCPR Article 20 and Tanzania's Constitution Article 13 equality guarantees, calling for bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ people.

Amnesty International's January 2024 report "We Are Facing Extinction" documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment. An OONI report from 2024 documents state-directed blocking of LGBTIQ websites and social networks in Tanzania, constraining LGBT access to information online.

A 2013 Human Rights Watch and Wake Up and Step Forward Coalition report documented torture of LGBT people in police custody, including a 19-year-old gay man arrested after leaving a nightclub in Mbeya who said police raped him and beat the soles of his feet with canes, electric wires and water pipes. In October 2017 the government deported staff of several HIV/AIDS groups on the basis of "promoting homosexuality", directly disrupting services. In 2018 a "witch hunt" against gay people was declared in Dar es Salaam, where gay men were forced to undergo anal examinations and torture; also in 2018 Paul Makonda, the Dar es Salaam Regional Commissioner, announced a 17-strong committee of police, lawyers and doctors to identify and punish homosexuals, scouring the internet for videos of supposedly LGBTQ people; the Foreign Ministry said the crackdown lacked government support and Denmark withheld 65 million kr (about US$9.8 million) in aid. The most recent documented incident in this record is from June 2024; no later instance is documented.

Government respect for freedom of speech and freedom of assembly is described as declining, and UN human rights defenders in Tanzania may not make public statements supporting tolerance for fear of reprisals. The 2018 broadcast content regulations bar inciting hatred on grounds of sexual preference; the online content regulations issued the same year banned such hate speech but were completely repealed by the 2020 online content regulations. The Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics for Media Professionals still bars hate speech, stereotypes and discrimination based on sexual orientation.

On the policy side, the 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines and Standards commit to services "regardless of age, parity, marital status, creed, race, color, or sexual preference", counselling "any woman, man, couple, or young person regardless of age"; the Nursing and Midwifery (practice) Regulations 2010 bar withholding nursing care based on sexual orientation; and the 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care require non-discriminatory care. No youth-specific healthcare provision beyond the age-inclusive family planning counselling language is stated.

There are no gay bars in Tanzania, although some places exist where gay men meet, and lesbians are less visible than gay men. Tanzania has a high HIV/AIDS rate with reportedly one million people infected.

The US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania identified the three most widespread problems as security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice, alongside discrimination based on sexual orientation and societal violence against persons with albinism; the same report details police custody abuse and describes Tanzania's human rights record as poor. An interview with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists from September 2020 documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy.

Activists Maria Sarungi Tsehai, Fatma Karume, Mwanahamisi Singano, Carol Ndosi, Zara Kay, Khalifa Said and Goodluck Haule have openly backed LGBTQ rights against officials such as Magufuli, Paul Makonda, Ally Hapi and Hamisi Kigwangalla, who pushed persecution.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Tanzania was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying profile documents Tanzania's criminalisation of same-sex activity with life imprisonment possible, but its specific claims could not be verified in this pass.

Rankings of incidents or problems by raw count, such as the US State Department's list of the three most widespread problems in Tanzania, track reported prevalence without per-capita denominators and should not be read as comparative risk measures against other jurisdictions.

Whether the specific penalties and provisions cited from the Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 and Zanzibar's Penal Code of 1934 (as amended 2004) remain in force as written, absent later amendment or judicial interpretation, is unresolved in this record.

The current operational status of the 2018 broadcast content regulations, the repealed 2020 online content regulations, and the Media Council of Tanzania's 2020 Code of Ethics as applied in practice is unresolved; the inventory documents their text and repeal history but not present enforcement.

Whether the non-discrimination language in the 2010 Nursing and Midwifery Regulations, 2013 National Family Planning Guidelines, and 2017 National Guidelines for Respectful and Compassionate Nursing and Midwifery Care is enforced against documented discrimination is not sourced here.

No current (post-2024) trans-specific violence statistics, incidence rates, or denominators are available in this inventory; the most recent documented incident is the June 2024 attack on Mauzinde, and no later instance is documented.
